title: In defence of idleness
text:
For most of my adult life, I have treated rest as something to be earned. A free afternoon had to be justified by a morning of hard work, and even holidays came with a reading list. I suspect I am not alone. In a culture that measures worth by output, doing nothing feels less like a pleasure than a minor moral failing, something to be confessed rather than enjoyed.

It was a broken ankle that forced me to reconsider. Confined to the sofa for six weeks, unable to commute, run or even stand at the kitchen counter, I expected to be miserable. For the first few days I was. I filled the hours with emails and half-hearted attempts at work, as if my value might drain away if I stopped. Then, slowly, something shifted. I re-read old letters, watched the clouds and, for the first time in years, did not know what day it was. Without anything to prove, I began to notice how rarely I had simply let my mind wander.

Psychologists have a name for what I was rediscovering. When we are not concentrating on a task, the brain does not switch off; a network of regions becomes more active, apparently helping us to connect memories, imagine the future and make sense of our experiences. Many of the ideas we describe as coming out of nowhere arrive during precisely these moments: in the shower, on a walk, while staring out of a train window. Far from being wasted time, idleness may be when some of our most important thinking takes place.

None of this will surprise anyone who has ever struggled with a problem at a desk, given up in frustration and found the solution an hour later while washing the dishes. What is surprising is how little room most of us leave for such moments. Every gap in the day, every queue and every bus journey, is now filled by a screen. We are rarely bored, and therefore rarely idle in the sense that matters.

Employers, too, are beginning to take notice. Some companies now encourage staff to take proper lunch breaks away from their desks, and a few have experimented with meeting-free afternoons. The motives are not entirely selfless: an exhausted workforce makes mistakes, and a team that never pauses is unlikely to come up with anything genuinely new. Still, it is a striking change from the days when the last person to leave the office was assumed to be the most committed.

I should be careful not to overstate my case. Idleness is a luxury that not everyone can afford; the single parent working two jobs does not need a lecture on the virtues of lying in a hammock. And there is a difference between rest that restores us and the kind of aimless scrolling that leaves us more tired than before. Doing nothing, it turns out, is a skill, and like any skill it has to be practised.

My ankle has long since healed, and I am back to my old routines. But I have kept one habit from those six weeks. Every afternoon, for twenty minutes, I sit by the window without a phone, a book or a plan. My colleagues, I suspect, think I am wasting time. I have come to think it is the most productive part of my day.

items.question: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that many people regard doing nothing as

options.A: a reward they have not deserved.
options.B: something slightly shameful.
options.C: a waste of a holiday.
options.D: a sign of good mental health.

items.evidence: doing nothing feels less like a pleasure than a minor moral failing
items.hint: Look at the words 'moral failing' and 'confessed'.
items.explanation: A 'minor moral failing' that has to be 'confessed' is something slightly shameful. Option A is tempting because rest has to be 'earned', but the key claim is about guilt, not about deserving a reward.

items.question: What does the writer say about the first days after the accident?

options.A: The writer found it impossible to do any work.
options.B: The writer immediately enjoyed the chance to rest.
options.C: The writer kept trying to be productive.
options.D: The writer was too unhappy to think clearly.

items.evidence: I filled the hours with emails and half-hearted attempts at work
items.hint: What did the writer fill the hours with at first?
items.explanation: In the first days the writer kept answering emails and trying to work 'as if my value might drain away'. The change only came later ('Then, slowly, something shifted').

items.question: According to the third paragraph, what happens when we are not concentrating on a task?

options.A: Our brains rest completely and recover energy.
options.B: We find it harder to remember past experiences.
options.C: We are more likely to make mistakes.
options.D: Certain parts of the brain become more active.

items.evidence: a network of regions becomes more active
items.hint: Does the brain 'switch off'?
items.explanation: The text says the brain does NOT switch off: 'a network of regions becomes more active'. It helps us connect memories, so B says the opposite.

items.question: The writer mentions washing the dishes in order to

options.A: illustrate a common experience of solving a problem away from the desk.
options.B: show that household tasks can be as tiring as office work.
options.C: suggest that people should share domestic work more fairly.
options.D: criticise people who give up too easily.

items.evidence: found the solution an hour later while washing the dishes
items.hint: What happens while the person is washing the dishes?
items.explanation: The example shows a familiar experience: giving up on a problem at a desk and solving it later while doing something else. It supports the idea that idle moments help us think.

items.question: What point does the writer make in the paragraph beginning 'I should be careful'?

options.A: Some forms of rest are more beneficial than others.
options.B: Everyone should be able to spend time in a hammock.
options.C: Idleness comes naturally to most people.
options.D: People with busy lives need idleness more than others.

items.evidence: there is a difference between rest that restores us and the kind of aimless scrolling that leaves us more tired than before
items.hint: The writer compares two kinds of 'doing nothing'.
items.explanation: The writer distinguishes rest that 'restores us' from scrolling that makes us more tired. C is wrong: doing nothing is described as 'a skill' that 'has to be practised'.

items.question: How does the writer feel about the afternoon habit described in the last paragraph?

options.A: embarrassed that colleagues might notice it
options.B: doubtful that it makes any real difference
options.C: convinced of its value despite how it may look to others
options.D: ready to give it up now that life is busy again

items.evidence: I have come to think it is the most productive part of my day.
items.hint: What do colleagues think, and what does the writer think?
items.explanation: Colleagues may think the writer is wasting time, but the writer considers it 'the most productive part of my day'. There is no sign of embarrassment or doubt.

title: Can data win the league?
text:
When I started writing about football twenty years ago, the most sophisticated statistic in the press box was the number of corners each team had won. Today, clubs employ teams of analysts who can tell you how far every player ran, how often he pressed an opponent and the probability that any given shot would end up in the net. As someone who once dismissed this sort of thing as spreadsheet football, I have had to eat a certain amount of humble pie.

The change has been most visible in recruitment. Clubs that cannot afford to compete for established stars have learned to use data to find undervalued players in smaller leagues, buying them cheaply and selling them on at a profit. Some of those players were later sold for ten times what their clubs had paid. Several of the most admired success stories of the past decade began with an analyst noticing something that the traditional scouting network had missed.

Data has changed coaching, too. Training sessions are now planned around detailed measurements of players' workloads, with the aim of reducing injuries, and set pieces are designed with the help of software that analyses thousands of previous corners and free kicks. Some of the improvements are tiny, but in a sport where a single goal can be worth millions, tiny improvements matter.

Yet the more time I spend with analysts, the more I am struck by how modest the best of them are about what numbers can do. One head of recruitment told me that data was a very good way of deciding which players to watch, and a very bad way of deciding which ones to buy. Statistics can show that a midfielder completes most of his passes; they are much less reliable at telling you whether he will cope with a hostile crowd, a new language or a manager who shouts.

There is also the problem of what gets measured. Actions that leave a trace in the data, such as shots, tackles and sprints, are easy to count. The things that often decide matches, such as the decision not to make a run that would have pulled a defender out of position, are almost invisible. A player who is brilliant at these quiet contributions can look ordinary on a spreadsheet, and a club that relies too heavily on the numbers risks letting him go. Analysts are working hard on these blind spots, but they are not easy to fix.

Supporters, meanwhile, have not always welcomed the new language. Phrases such as expected goals are now used on television to explain why a team that lost was, in some sense, unlucky. To many fans, this sounds like an excuse. A match is not decided by the chances a team should have scored, they point out, but by the ones it actually did. Others simply find it dull.

My own view has settled somewhere in the middle. Data has made football smarter, and clubs that ignore it do so at their peril. But the game remains stubbornly human. It is played by people who get nervous, fall out with their coaches and occasionally do something no model could have predicted. The analysts I most admire understand this perfectly; it is some of their more enthusiastic admirers in the media who sometimes forget it. That, in the end, is why we watch.

items.question: Why does the writer mention corners in the first paragraph?

options.A: to show how limited football statistics used to be
options.B: to suggest that corners are more important than people think
options.C: to criticise journalists who rely on statistics
options.D: to explain why the writer became interested in data

items.evidence: the most sophisticated statistic in the press box was the number of corners each team had won
items.hint: Compare the statistics of twenty years ago with those of today.
items.explanation: If counting corners was 'the most sophisticated statistic', statistics were very basic then. The contrast with today's detailed data is the point.

items.question: What does the writer mean by saying 'I have had to eat a certain amount of humble pie'?

options.A: The writer has stopped writing about football.
options.B: The writer has become less interested in the game.
options.C: The writer has had to admit to having been wrong.
options.D: The writer has learned to use statistics at work.

items.evidence: As someone who once dismissed this sort of thing as spreadsheet football, I have had to eat a certain amount of humble pie.
items.hint: What did the writer once think about data?
items.explanation: To 'eat humble pie' is to admit you were wrong. The writer once dismissed data as 'spreadsheet football' and now accepts its value.

items.question: According to the writer, how have some clubs used data in recruitment?

options.A: to replace their scouting networks entirely
options.B: to identify players whose value was not recognised
options.C: to persuade established stars to join them
options.D: to decide which players to sell to bigger clubs

items.evidence: use data to find undervalued players in smaller leagues
items.hint: What kind of players do these clubs look for?
items.explanation: 'Undervalued players' are those whose quality other clubs had not recognised. The text says analysts noticed things scouts had missed, not that scouting was replaced (A).

items.question: The head of recruitment quoted in the fourth paragraph believes that data

options.A: should be the main factor in buying decisions.
options.B: is useful at an early stage of choosing players.
options.C: cannot be trusted at all.
options.D: is better at judging character than skill.

items.evidence: a very good way of deciding which players to watch, and a very bad way of deciding which ones to buy
items.hint: Data is good for deciding what, and bad for deciding what?
items.explanation: Data helps decide which players to watch (an early stage), but not which ones to buy. It is not useless (C), and the text says it is poor at judging how players will cope (D).

items.question: What problem with data does the writer describe in the paragraph beginning 'There is also the problem'?

options.A: Some valuable contributions are hard to measure.
options.B: Players change their behaviour when they know they are being measured.
options.C: Clubs collect far too much information.
options.D: Analysts disagree about which actions matter most.

items.evidence: The things that often decide matches, such as the decision not to make a run that would have pulled a defender out of position, are almost invisible
items.hint: Which contributions leave no trace in the data?
items.explanation: Quiet contributions that often decide matches are 'almost invisible' in the data, so a brilliant player can look ordinary on a spreadsheet.

items.question: What is the writer's overall view of data in football?

options.A: It has spoiled the game for supporters.
options.B: It will eventually be able to predict most results.
options.C: It matters more in coaching than in recruitment.
options.D: It is useful but cannot explain everything about the sport.

items.evidence: Data has made football smarter, and clubs that ignore it do so at their peril. But the game remains stubbornly human.
items.hint: Read the last paragraph: the writer's view is 'somewhere in the middle'.
items.explanation: The writer accepts that data has made football smarter but insists that the game 'remains stubbornly human' and unpredictable. Some fans dislike it (A), but that is not the writer's overall view.

title: What failure really taught me
text:
Seven years ago, the company I had spent four years building went bankrupt. Thirty people lost their jobs, investors lost their money, and I lost, for a while, any sense of who I was. Friends told me that every successful entrepreneur has a failure behind them. At the time, I would have given anything to hear that it was all part of a valuable learning experience. Today, now that I run a business that is doing rather well, people expect me to say exactly that. I am not sure it is true.

There is a fashionable idea, particularly in the technology industry, that failure is something to be celebrated. Conferences hold sessions in which founders cheerfully recount their disasters, and investors claim to prefer entrepreneurs who have failed fast. Some even put their failed companies on their CVs as if they were medals. I understand the intention. Fear of failure stops many good ideas from ever being tried, and it is healthy to admit that most new businesses do not survive. But the celebration often skips over the cost, and the cost is rarely borne by the person on the stage.

What I learned from my failure was not, in the main, the lessons I had expected. I did not discover some hidden flaw in my strategy; with hindsight, the strategy was reasonable, and we were simply overtaken by a larger competitor with deeper pockets. What I learned was more personal. I learned how much I had tied my sense of worth to my job title, and how few of the people I called friends were interested in me once I no longer had one. It was a humbling discovery. For months I avoided social events altogether, unable to answer the simple question of what I did.

I also learned something about the people who stayed. My former finance director, who had every reason to be angry with me, phoned every week for a year simply to ask how I was. She never once mentioned the money she had invested herself. When I eventually started again, she was the first person I hired. If there is a lesson in failure worth sharing, it is that it shows you who your real allies are, and that is information no business plan can provide.

None of this makes me grateful for what happened. I would rather have learned these things in a less painful way, and I would certainly rather the thirty people who worked for me had not paid the price for my education. When young founders ask me whether they should be afraid of failure, I tell them they should take it seriously, which is not the same thing. Fear paralyses; respect makes you careful. The distinction may sound small, but it has shaped every decision I have made since.

My current company is run more cautiously than my first. We grow more slowly, we borrow less, and I spend far more time worrying about the people who depend on us. Our growth targets are modest, and we review them every few months. We also have a rule that nobody's job depends on a single customer or a single investor. Some investors find this frustrating. I can live with that. I would rather build something that lasts than give another cheerful talk about the time it all went wrong.

items.question: In the first paragraph, what does the writer say people now expect?

options.A: that the writer will describe the bankruptcy as a useful experience
options.B: that the writer will explain how the company could have been saved
options.C: that the writer will apologise to the investors who lost money
options.D: that the writer will give advice to people starting a business

items.evidence: people expect me to say exactly that
items.hint: What does 'exactly that' refer back to?
items.explanation: 'Exactly that' refers to the idea that failure was 'a valuable learning experience'. Now that the writer is successful, people expect this message.

items.question: What does the writer criticise in the second paragraph?

options.A: the fear that prevents people from starting businesses
options.B: the way the costs of failure are often ignored
options.C: investors who refuse to support failed entrepreneurs
options.D: conferences that only invite successful founders

items.evidence: the celebration often skips over the cost
items.hint: The writer 'understands the intention', but what is missing?
items.explanation: The writer's criticism is that celebrating failure 'skips over the cost', which is usually paid by others. The writer actually agrees that fear of failure can be harmful (A).

items.question: According to the writer, the company failed mainly because

options.A: its strategy was badly flawed.
options.B: the writer was too focused on status.
options.C: a better-funded rival was more successful.
options.D: the staff lost confidence in the writer.

items.evidence: we were simply overtaken by a larger competitor with deeper pockets
items.hint: Did the writer find a flaw in the strategy?
items.explanation: A competitor 'with deeper pockets' had more money. The writer says the strategy was reasonable (not A); the focus on status (B) was a personal lesson, not the cause of failure.

items.question: What does the example of the former finance director illustrate?

options.A: Failure reveals who is genuinely loyal.
options.B: Colleagues should never become friends.
options.C: Staff are often angrier than they admit.
options.D: It is important to hire experienced people.

items.evidence: it shows you who your real allies are
items.hint: How did the finance director behave after the failure?
items.explanation: The finance director phoned every week despite having reason to be angry, showing she was a real ally. The writer concludes that failure 'shows you who your real allies are'.

items.question: What distinction does the writer make when talking to young founders?

options.A: between failing quickly and failing slowly
options.B: between personal and professional failure
options.C: between being afraid of failure and taking it seriously
options.D: between failures that are their fault and those that are not

items.evidence: they should take it seriously, which is not the same thing
items.hint: 'Fear paralyses; respect makes you careful.'
items.explanation: The writer tells founders to take failure seriously rather than to fear it: fear stops you acting, while respect makes you careful.

items.question: How does the writer feel about running the current company cautiously?

options.A: worried that it may cause the company to fail
options.B: embarrassed by how slowly the company is growing
options.C: keen to change the approach in the future
options.D: content, despite some investors' frustration

items.evidence: Some investors find this frustrating. I can live with that.
items.hint: What does 'I can live with that' tell you?
items.explanation: 'I can live with that' shows the writer accepts the investors' frustration and is happy with the cautious approach, preferring to 'build something that lasts'.

title: The slow way to Bilbao
text:
Last autumn, I travelled from London to Bilbao by train. It took two days, three changes and rather more patience than I had anticipated. A flight would have taken under two hours and, booked early enough, cost considerably less. When I told friends what I was planning, most assumed I was either afraid of flying or making some kind of point. They were wrong on both counts. In fact, my reasons were more selfish than either. I also wanted to see the countryside I had flown over so many times.

I had grown tired of the airport. Not of flying itself, which still strikes me as something close to a miracle, but of everything that surrounds it: the queues, the security checks, the overpriced sandwiches and the strange sense of being nowhere in particular. Airports are designed to be the same everywhere, and after a while I found that I could not remember which one I was in. A railway station, by contrast, belongs unmistakably to its city. Arriving at a great station, with its high glass roof and noisy cafés, feels like the beginning of a story.

The journey itself was not without its frustrations. My first train was delayed, which meant a nervous dash across Paris to catch the connection, and a strike in France forced me to spend an unplanned night in Bordeaux. Yet even these setbacks had their compensations. The unexpected evening in Bordeaux turned out to be one of the highlights of the trip, and I would never have seen the city had everything gone to plan. I ate in a small restaurant recommended by the hotel receptionist and walked along the river until midnight.

What struck me most was how differently time passes on a train. On a plane, the hours are something to be endured: you sit, you wait, you arrive. On a train, the journey becomes part of the experience. I watched the landscape change from the flat fields of northern France to the vineyards of the south and finally the green hills of the Basque Country. At one point, an elderly couple from Toulouse shared their lunch with me and insisted on teaching me a few words of Occitan. I read, I slept, I talked to strangers. By the time I arrived, I felt that I had genuinely travelled, rather than simply been transported.

I am aware, of course, that not everyone has two days to spare. For a business trip or a short break, the train will often be impractical, and until European rail companies make international tickets easier to book, many travellers will be put off before they start. Booking a single ticket that covered the whole route proved impossible, and some sections, I discovered, are better served by night buses than by trains. I spent a frustrating evening comparing websites in three languages, and even then I was not sure I had found the cheapest fares.

Environmental considerations played a part in my decision, but I would be misleading readers if I claimed they were the main one. Flying produces far more emissions than travelling by rail, and that matters to me. The truth is that I took the train because I wanted to enjoy getting there. For anyone with the time, I would recommend it wholeheartedly; just be sure to pack a good book, a spare phone charger and a generous supply of patience.

items.question: What does the writer say about friends' reactions to the plan?

options.A: They misunderstood the writer's real reasons.
options.B: They offered to join the writer on the trip.
options.C: They thought the journey would be too expensive.
options.D: They admired the writer's concern for the environment.

items.evidence: They were wrong on both counts.
items.hint: What did the friends assume, and were they right?
items.explanation: Friends assumed the writer was afraid of flying or making a point, but 'They were wrong on both counts': the real reasons were different.

items.question: What does the writer suggest about airports in the second paragraph?

options.A: They have improved a great deal in recent years.
options.B: They make flying more frightening than it should be.
options.C: They have no real connection to the places where they are.
options.D: They are more comfortable than railway stations.

items.evidence: Airports are designed to be the same everywhere
items.hint: Contrast airports with stations, which belong 'unmistakably to its city'.
items.explanation: Because airports are the same everywhere, they give a sense of 'being nowhere in particular', unlike stations, which belong to their city.

items.question: The writer describes the night in Bordeaux as

options.A: an unwelcome delay that spoiled the trip.
options.B: a positive result of an unplanned change.
options.C: the reason the writer missed a connection.
options.D: a planned stop to break up the journey.

items.evidence: The unexpected evening in Bordeaux turned out to be one of the highlights of the trip
items.hint: Was the stop planned? Was it a good or bad experience?
items.explanation: The night in Bordeaux was caused by a strike (unplanned) but became 'one of the highlights of the trip'.

items.question: What contrast does the writer draw in the fourth paragraph?

options.A: between the comfort of planes and trains
options.B: between the landscapes of France and Spain
options.C: between talking to strangers and reading alone
options.D: between travelling and simply being moved from place to place

items.evidence: I felt that I had genuinely travelled, rather than simply been transported
items.hint: Look at the last sentence of the paragraph.
items.explanation: On a plane you are simply 'transported'; on a train the journey becomes part of the experience, so the writer feels they have 'genuinely travelled'.

items.question: What problem with international rail travel does the writer mention?

options.A: Trains are often too crowded.
options.B: Fares change too often.
options.C: Buying tickets is unnecessarily complicated.
options.D: Staff rarely speak other languages.

items.evidence: until European rail companies make international tickets easier to book
items.hint: What did the writer spend 'a frustrating evening' doing?
items.explanation: Booking was difficult: no single ticket covered the route, and the writer compared websites in three languages. This puts many travellers off.

items.question: What does the writer say about the environmental reasons for the trip?

options.A: They were less important than the pleasure of the journey.
options.B: They were the writer's main motivation.
options.C: They are exaggerated by rail companies.
options.D: They should persuade everyone to stop flying.

items.evidence: The truth is that I took the train because I wanted to enjoy getting there.
items.hint: Were environmental reasons 'the main one'?
items.explanation: The environment 'played a part', but the writer admits the main reason was wanting to enjoy the journey. B is the opposite of what the text says.
